Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Vignette:
Elias Vance had spent fifteen years as a session and touring musician, moving between cities and stages, until the evening three years ago when a venue manager invited him into a dimly lit administrative office under the pretense of reviewing a contract. What happened inside remains fractured for him. He had come to believe that his mind would not let him hold the full sequence; he could push the memory away before he could fully recall it, yet certain moments surfaced with jarring clarity: the sharp, sweet scent of a specific cologne, the sudden lunge of the man’s arm, the dull impact that split his lip and left a coppery smear on his cuff. Other stretches were completely blank, leaving him unable to tell a coherent story of what happened even to himself. When the manager stepped away, Elias had fled, but the fragments did not fade. Instead, they hardened into a quiet, persistent dread that followed him home. In the weeks that followed, Elias found himself retreating from the very spaces that once defined his life. He stopped attending band rehearsals, avoided social contacts he had shared drinks and laughter with before the event, and declined every offer to play live venues. He had come to believe that the only places he felt safe were the soundproof walls of his home studio and the master bedroom, a limited number of rooms that he began to guard with rigid routine. When his wife asked him to attend a mutual friend’s dinner, he refused, citing exhaustion, though what frightened him most was the thought of entering a space where strangers might occupy seats of authority. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger about the refusals, swallowing every flash of frustration until it settled into a dense, immovable fatigue. His days narrowed to composing on his guitar and monitoring the house, his posture forever braced for the threat in movements: a door opening too quickly, a floorboard creaking, a hand reaching toward him. Now, at fifty-six, Elias maintains a precarious routine in the daily environment of his home office. His career has shifted entirely to solitary, home-based composition, a quiet retreat that keeps him from the rehearsal halls and booking offices he once navigated without hesitation. He books remote sessions through email, carefully avoiding phone calls from venue promoters or union representatives, whom he equates with uniformed authority. Yesterday, while restringing an acoustic guitar on his workbench, a minor slip of the tuning peg nicked his thumb. When he saw the bead of blood welling on his skin, he dropped the instrument and backed against the desk, his breath catching as the visual cue unlocked a sudden, visceral alarm. The irritability that followed was immediate; when his wife entered the room to ask about dinner, he snapped at her to leave him alone before he could stop himself. He had come to believe that his only defense was to never let the anger surface again, so he sat rigidly in the corner of the room until his breathing slowed. What finally brought him to seek help was not a single breakdown, but the slow erosion of the life he had built. He had hoped to return to the stage, to reconnect with the musicians he had abandoned, but the gap between who he was and who he had become had grown too wide to cross alone. Sitting in the therapist’s office now, Elias clutched his notebook, certain that if he could only piece together the missing fragments of that night, he might finally lower his guard. He did not know how to make sense of the cologne that still made his stomach turn, or the sudden movements that still hijacked his body, but he was hoping, for the first time in years, to stop running from the spaces between the memories.
